sample_unit: base prompts (of >3.4 million total prompts across 20 LLMs)

links.outcome: LLM susceptibility to false claims under neutral versus logical-fallacy rephrased prompts
links.effect: Base susceptibility was 31.7% (50,108/158,000). Fallacy framings changed it: appeal to popularity 11.9% (-19.8 points), slippery slope 33.9% (+2.2), appeal to authority 34.6% (+2.9); eight of ten framings reduced or did not change the rate.
links.quote: Eight of ten fallacy framings significantly reduced or did not change that rate, led by appeal to popularity (susceptibility 11·9%; difference of -19·8 percentage points; p<0·0001); only the slippery-slope prompt (33·9%; difference of 2·2 percentage points; p<0·0001) and the appeal-to-authority prompt (34·6%; difference of 2·9 percentage points; p<0·0001) increased it.

links.outcome: Rate at which LLMs accept fabricated medical content in clinical notes, social media, and vignettes
links.effect: LLMs were susceptible in 50,108 (31.7%) of 158,000 base prompts; real hospital notes with an inserted false recommendation 46.1% (46,108/100,000); social media 8.9% (2,479/28,000); Gemma-3-4B-it 63.6% (5,023/7,900).
links.quote: Across all models and corpora, LLMs were susceptible to fabricated data in 50 108 (31·7%) of 158 000 base prompts.

links.outcome: Model detection of misinformation and logical-fallacy rhetoric in prompts
links.effect: LLMs accepted fabricated claims in 31.7% of base prompts. GPT models were least susceptible and most accurate at fallacy detection; other models such as Gemma-3-4B-it were susceptible in 63.6% (5,023/7,900).
links.quote: Performance varied by model: GPT models were the least susceptible and most accurate at fallacy detection, whereas others, such as Gemma-3-4B-it, showed 63·6% (5023 of 7900) susceptibility.

screen.reason: The study benchmarks the susceptibility of 20 LLMs to medical misinformation and logical fallacies across prompt variants, but does not test an organizational deployment practice or guardrail implementation.
